channel.title: Polygon Digital
channel.description: Market analysis with conviction. We tell you what we think is happening and why it matters.

item.title: The key man: Nvidia's spy scandal is a governance trade, not a chip trade
item.description: On November 8 Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, and the board opened an independent investigation into reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The stock fell for two sessions, lost on the order of $400 billion of value, and drew a securities class action within a day. Nothing about the order book changed. What got repriced is the one input nobody models: the man who runs the company, and the Washington channel that only he holds.

item.title: The borrowed hand: America bought yen for the first time since 1998, and the market gave half of it back in five days
item.description: On July 30 the yen touched 163.73, its weakest against the dollar since 1986. Over the next two sessions Tokyo bought roughly ¥13.8 trillion of its own currency, and on the second day the US Treasury bought alongside it, the first joint yen purchase since 1998. By August 10 the yen had given back about 46% of the move. The interesting thing is not that intervention failed. It is what the failure tells you about why the yen is falling in the first place.

item.title: The crown jewel: FIFA priced 20% of the World Cup and unpriced it in four days
item.description: On July 28 FIFA proposed selling roughly 20% of a new subsidiary holding the commercial rights to the World Cup, at a $20 billion valuation, to a group led by Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital. Four days later it was dead. The terms were not the problem. This is what the collapse says about outside capital in sport, and why the answer to "is private equity good for the teams" is usually a question about duration and consent instead.

item.title: The forced seller: how a fund up 439% got liquidated in six days
item.description: On July 24 Situational Awareness told investors it was up 439% net for the first half of 2026. On July 30, before the open, it sold its entire public equity portfolio to Citadel in one block trade to meet margin calls. The month came in at minus 67%. The thesis was not wrong. The financing was. Here is the mechanism, and the tape print that proves the assets were never the problem.

item.title: The margin call: how Korea's leveraged chip trade liquidated 1.2 million people
item.description: The KOSPI doubled in six months, then gave back more in one month than it did in 1997 or 2008. The index number is not the story. The story is that 1.2 million retail margin accounts got called and up to 460,000 were sold out by their own brokers. Here is the machine that did it, and an interactive chart that shows you exactly where a levered position dies.

item.title: Kimi K3 did not undercut the frontier, it joined it: the largest open model ever and the price of intelligence
item.description: Moonshot released Kimi K3 on July 16 and published the weights this morning. The model placed fourth of 189 on the independent intelligence index, and it listed at $3 per million input tokens, roughly triple what the previous Kimi costs. Moonshot did not raise anyone's prices. It launched a model a full weight class up and charged accordingly. Here is what that says about what a unit of intelligence is actually worth, why the deflation everyone is waiting for arrives through downloads rather than rate cards, and why the grade of the barrel matters more than the price of it.

item.title: The Kimi shock: China's largest open model reprices the AI trade
item.description: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 this month, a 2.8 trillion parameter open-weight model that lands in the top four on the public leaderboards while pricing at a fraction of the closed frontier. Chip and AI stocks sold off within hours in what traders called a second DeepSeek moment. Here is our read on what actually changed, and why the selloff was never really about chips.

item.title: The gas behind the boom: how data centers and LNG are fighting for the same molecule
item.description: AI data centers cannot wait five years for a grid connection, so hyperscalers are building their own gas power plants on site. US data center gas demand is heading from near zero to somewhere between 3 and 6 billion cubic feet a day by 2030. At the same time LNG exporters are bidding for the same supply. Here is our read on how much gas the boom burns, and who gets paid to supply it.

item.title: The DeepSeek discount: China's AI is closing the gap, and it costs a tenth as much
item.description: DeepSeek is preparing an IPO at a rumoured ~$71B valuation, and China's models now land within single digits of the Western frontier while charging 5–30x less. The interesting question for a North American reader is not whether to buy the stock. It is whether that price gap is a real arbitrage or a trap. Here is our read.

item.title: The gigawatt land grab: why Meta went to Alberta, and what it costs
item.description: Meta just broke ground on a CAD $13B, 1-gigawatt AI data centre in rural Alberta, its first in Canada and 33rd worldwide. Strip away the ribbon-cutting and it is a case study in the real bottleneck of the AI boom: not chips, not talent, but power, land, and the political will to permit both. Here is our read on who wins.

item.title: The measuring stick: why the dollar, not the Strait of Hormuz, may be pulling oil down
item.description: Oil has round-tripped its entire war spike even though Hormuz transit is still choked, and gold, silver, Bitcoin, and megacap stocks fell right alongside it. One underappreciated variable ties them together: a strengthening US dollar. Here is the case for watching the measuring stick, not the barrel.

item.title: The token paradox: AI's economy is exploding, deflating, and barely profitable
item.description: Token volumes are up hundreds of times over, the price of intelligence is collapsing ~10x a year, growth is already decelerating, and almost no one selling tokens is making money. Here is who actually wins.
